title: COP31: priorities, finance and methane — views from UK experts
label: 26 October 2026 · COP31 prospects
summary: UK business, NGO and think‑tank experts told the Environmental Audit Committee that COP31 is likely to be technical rather than landmark, and stressed four practical priorities: protect the science and global stocktake process, elevate adaptation and cooling, push electrification while not avoiding tough fossil‑fuel discussions, and fix how climate finance is sequenced and delivered. They highlighted the rise of coalitions outside the UNFCCC, the need for clarity from the Turkish–Australian Presidency and the UK, and urged rapid action on methane and other short‑lived pollutants with finance and safeguards for solutions such as biomethane.

chapters.title: Opening: where COP31 stands
chapters.takeaway: Experts expect technical talks rather than big political breakthroughs; they want clarity from the Presidencies and protection of the science that feeds the global stocktake.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Welcome. Please introduce yourselves and give a short view of where COP31 negotiations are heading.

turns.speaker: Kim O’Dowd
turns.text: I lead methane work at the Environmental Investigation Agency. COP31 lacks clarity on how the UNFCCC will interact with many parallel initiatives—like the Santa Marta energy transition conference and the global methane and cooling pledges.

turns.speaker: Pelin Zorlu
turns.text: I’m at Chatham House. We don’t expect landmark decisions—more technical negotiations. Key benchmarks are protecting the global stocktake process and ensuring science (IPCC findings) informs it; recent blocks to IPCC progress are worrying and need unblocking by Presidencies and the UK.

turns.speaker: Tania Kumar
turns.text: I represent the CBI. This year’s context—new energy shocks, e.g. the Hormuz disruption—means energy security will be central. The UK can help build longer‑term diplomatic consensus across COP, G7 and G20 over several years, not just at one COP.

chapters.title: Diplomacy and the rise of coalitions
chapters.takeaway: Climate diplomacy now spans trade, security and industrial policy, and we see more implementation coalitions outside the UNFCCC; those can help but need coordination and inclusivity.

turns.speaker: Sojan Joseph
turns.text: What is driving climate diplomacy in 2026, including negotiating outside the UNFCCC?

turns.speaker: Pelin Zorlu
turns.text: Climate diplomacy now intersects with economics, energy security and trade—look at measures like CBAM, Korea’s green package, and the IRA. Energy shocks push countries to see renewables as strategic independence.

turns.speaker: Kim O’Dowd
turns.text: We’re seeing two‑tier multilateralism: the UNFCCC stays for consensus and signals, while coalitions of the willing drive implementation. That’s useful, but we must remember the UNFCCC’s core functions and ensure other initiatives connect with it.

turns.speaker: Tania Kumar
turns.text: Business plays a diplomatic role by showing what’s practically investable and by helping Governments build stable policy models—CFDs and the RAB model are often cited by other countries as successful examples.

turns.speaker: Sarah Gibson
turns.text: Do the Ambassador and High Commissioner miss anything in their approach?

turns.speaker: Kim O’Dowd
turns.text: Methane—especially from the energy sector—needs continued prominence, and agriculture mitigation is under-addressed; both deserve policy attention, not just research.

turns.speaker: Pelin Zorlu
turns.text: We need clarity on how electrification initiatives will connect to other funds and whether there’s a clear TAFF (transition away from fossil fuels) roadmap from the Presidencies and partners.

turns.speaker: Tania Kumar
turns.text: There are many new alliances; business wants consolidation so efforts aren’t scattered—prioritise where coalitions can add value and build bridges across Presidencies.

chapters.title: Money and sequencing: making finance work
chapters.takeaway: Experts stressed that more money is needed but, crucially, finance must be sequenced and coordinated so countries can plan, build policy, then attract private investment.

turns.speaker: Bill Esterson
turns.text: Is business’s role in climate diplomacy mainly about finance, or wider?

turns.speaker: Tania Kumar
turns.text: It’s wider: businesses showcase green growth opportunities, advise on policy tools that attract investment, and help make projects bankable. Private capital is essential, but it must be used where it fits in the broader financing stack.

turns.speaker: Bill Esterson
turns.text: Kim, what’s the equivalent role for environmental groups?

turns.speaker: Kim O’Dowd
turns.text: NGOs bring expertise to negotiations and often host secretariats for coalitions. That helps implementation. But as more entry points open, smaller NGOs and some Global South actors risk being excluded unless access is safeguarded.

turns.speaker: Sojan Joseph
turns.text: How is finance driving climate diplomacy among major players?

turns.speaker: Pelin Zorlu
turns.text: Public finance can’t do it alone; the UK’s EMDE taskforce is helpful to lower perceived costs of capital for emerging markets and unlock private investment, but access to affordable capital remains uneven.

turns.speaker: Kim O’Dowd
turns.text: Beyond quantity, we need an organised architecture: countries currently face many separate funds and instruments. Sequencing matters—start with grants for planning, then de‑risking instruments to attract private capital. The UK could help push practical linkages between existing funds.

chapters.title: Methane, cooling, electrification and UK priorities
chapters.takeaway: Methane and other super‑pollutants, cooling solutions and electrification are practical focus areas; the UK should lead on methane, cooling action, Electrify Now and industrial decarbonisation, with careful safeguards for biomethane.

turns.speaker: John Whitby
turns.text: Should COP31 focus on getting back to 1.5°C?

turns.speaker: Pelin Zorlu
turns.text: Framing will be about implementing the Paris goals. UNEP says a temporary overshoot of 1.5°C is likely in the next few years, but that doesn’t invalidate the target—every fraction of a degree avoided matters.

turns.speaker: John Whitby
turns.text: What should the UK prioritise at COP31?

turns.speaker: Kim O’Dowd
turns.text: Keep UK methane leadership—energy‑sector methane is waste and must be addressed. Also push finance for super‑pollutant action (the CCAC’s country action accelerator needs more funding) and a cooling agenda aligned with adaptation.

turns.speaker: Tania Kumar
turns.text: Electrification is a UK priority—Electrify Now aims to show practical steps for demand electrification as well as power. Industrial decarbonisation is also essential to avoid deindustrialisation while delivering the transition.

turns.speaker: Pelin Zorlu
turns.text: The UK is seen as an honest broker and coalition builder; it should pick the highest‑impact initiatives to lead and maintain the multilateral basics.

turns.speaker: Bill Esterson
turns.text: On methane and continued gas use: how do we reduce methane emissions while gas remains part of many energy systems?

turns.speaker: Kim O’Dowd
turns.text: We need both a sprint and a marathon—rapid methane cuts and a long‑term energy transition. For biomethane, safeguards matter: avoid incentives that increase herd sizes or cause land‑use harm. Also regulate monitoring, reporting and verification so biomethane doesn’t leak as much as fossil gas.

turns.speaker: Pelin Zorlu
turns.text: Not all biofuels or biomethane are equal—sustainability and economic viability depend on country context. Policies that mandate biofuel blends risk trade‑offs with food security and forests if poorly designed.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you all. Your evidence will help shape our work and is timely ahead of Antalya.
